label: Astra Low
what: Tracks missed cleaning tasks through correction and recheck.
avatar: Commercial cleaning owners managing recurring office sites.
moat: Client-specific standards and a history of fixes that worked.
proved: A correction had to be rechecked before the job could close. The closed state survived a refresh.
gap: No X evidence. More elapsed time and processed tokens than Medium.
takeaway: Use this as a reminder that Low can still produce a complete workflow. Lower effort does not guarantee a smaller total job.

label: Astra Medium
what: Prices extra cleaning work and records client acceptance.
avatar: Commercial cleaning owners with written service agreements.
moat: Accurate scope records and estimates improved by actual jobs.
proved: Changing labor from 45 to 60 minutes changed the monthly proposal from $164 to $212. A simulated acceptance and the new amount survived refresh.
gap: No X evidence. The lightest canvas by element count.
takeaway: My starting pick for this brief. It delivered a checked workflow and a useful plan in the shortest observed time.

label: Astra High
what: Reassigns visits when a cleaning crew cannot work.
avatar: Residential cleaning owners juggling crews and appointments.
moat: Company-specific constraints and outcomes that improve scheduling.
proved: An impossible two-hour job inside a one-hour window was rejected. Valid reassignment saved correctly and left four other visits untouched.
gap: Travel used a fixed allowance, not live route optimization.
takeaway: A useful next setting to test when your job has interacting constraints. The value here came from the behavior it handled.

label: Astra Extra High
what: Takes remodeling extras from approval into billing.
avatar: Small remodeling owners losing track of chargeable extras.
moat: Tailored scope checks informed by what got approved, billed and paid.
proved: A new labor rate flowed through a $530 total, approval and a ready-to-bill row. Revision 1 survived refresh.
gap: More elapsed time than High. Its X counterexample was participant-read; the producer could not independently reopen it.
takeaway: Read counterevidence before buying the business idea. An existing Grok plus open-source accounting workaround challenged the proposed product.

label: Astra Max
what: Keeps an extra job’s scope, price and approval in one record.
avatar: Residential remodeler owners with teams of 2–10 people.
moat: An adopted job-site routine, assisted setup and bookkeeper referrals.
proved: Labor of $275.25 plus materials of $84.75 became exactly $360. The simulated approval persisted.
gap: Longest run. A native export download was not independently verified.
takeaway: Useful depth showed up in exact cents, approval state and revision rules. These are better checks than counting UI polish.

label: Sol High
what: Plans recovery when delays disrupt a service route.
avatar: Owner-dispatchers of recurring service firms with 2–20 staff.
moat: Recovery outcomes, maintained rules and accountable support.
proved: Step progression and a resolved state persisted.
gap: Selecting Split with Crew 1 did not change the next summary: it still showed a different plan and fixed outcome numbers.
takeaway: Keep Sol in your comparison, then test whether choices actually change results. Low processed usage does not compensate for a broken decision path.

label: Astra Ultra
what: Records and agrees remodeling additions before work starts.
avatar: Small residential remodeling owners handling frequent extras.
moat: Trade-specific setup and a proven routine, improved by real outcomes.
proved: A newly created custom $200 change required an approval note. Its title, scope, total and approval persisted.
gap: Three child agents added 7.12M processed tokens. This is a separate delegation-enabled condition.
takeaway: Use delegation when independent research or checking lanes have real value. Here it produced deeper competitor workflow research, not a dramatically different product.
